findings.title: Negative offset passed to Django queryset will raise AssertionError
findings.body: When `enable_advanced_features` is True and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` for negative slice indices. The comment on line 876 claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. Any request that provides a cursor with a negative offset (which is user-controlled via the cursor query parameter parsed by `Cursor.from_string`) will cause an unhandled 500 error.

findings.title: User-controlled query parameter enables code path that crashes with crafted cursor
findings.body: The `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter combined with a crafted cursor containing a negative offset value (e.g., `cursor=0:-5:0`) will trigger the negative-offset code path in `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, causing an unhandled AssertionError. While gated behind `is_superuser` or `has_global_access`, this is still a denial-of-service vector for privileged users and indicates the feature was not tested with adversarial inputs.

findings.title: BasePaginator.get_result behavioral change allows negative offset for is_prev cursors across all subclasses
findings.body: The change from `queryset[offset:stop]` to `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` means that when `cursor.is_prev` is True, a negative offset is passed directly to the queryset slice. Since `Cursor.from_string` parses user-supplied input with `int(bits[1])`, a negative value can be injected. This affects all BasePaginator subclasses (Paginator, DateTimePaginator), not just the new OptimizedCursorPaginator. Previously, the same negative offset would also fail, but the misleading comment ('This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions') suggests the author believed this was safe.

findings.title: zpopmin evicts lowest-scored (earliest end_timestamp) spans, potentially removing the root span
findings.body: The eviction logic `redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000)` removes members with the lowest scores. Since scores are `end_timestamp_precise`, this evicts spans with the earliest end timestamps. A root/segment span may have an earlier end timestamp than its children (e.g., if it finishes before long-running child spans). If the root span is evicted, the segment will be flushed without a root span: `has_root_span` will be false, the flush timeout will use `span_buffer_timeout_secs` instead of `span_buffer_root_timeout_secs`, and `is_segment` will never be set to True for any span in the output, corrupting downstream segment data.

findings.title: Removal of max_segment_spans check during flush creates inconsistency with existing data
findings.body: The old code enforced `max_segment_spans` during `_load_segment_data` (flush time), rejecting segments that exceeded the limit. This check is removed, relying solely on the Lua script's eviction at insert time. However, segments already stored in Redis before this deployment may exceed 1000 spans and will now be flushed without any size guard. Additionally, the `max_segment_spans` parameter still exists in the constructor (line 150) but is no longer used, creating a confusing dead parameter.

findings.title: Direct dictionary access on end_timestamp_precise will crash consumer if field is missing
findings.body: `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` uses direct key access rather than `.get()`. If any span message lacks this field (due to schema evolution, a producer bug, or a malformed message), the consumer will raise a KeyError and crash. Other optional fields in the same block use `.get()` (e.g., `val.get("parent_span_id")`). Consider using `val.get("end_timestamp_precise", 0.0)` or handling the KeyError gracefully to avoid consumer death on a single bad message.

findings.title: __reduce__ passes redis_ttl as the segment_page_size positional argument
findings.body: `__reduce__` returns `(SpansBuffer, (self.assigned_shards, self.span_buffer_timeout_secs, self.span_buffer_root_timeout_secs, self.redis_ttl))`. The constructor's 4th positional parameter is `segment_page_size`, not `redis_ttl`. When this object is unpickled (e.g., in multiprocessing), `redis_ttl` (default 3600) will be used as `segment_page_size`, and `redis_ttl` will fall back to its default. This is a pre-existing bug but is relevant because the PR changes the data stored in Redis (sorted sets vs sets), making correct pickling more important for the multiprocessing path (`num_processes != 1`).

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator is a near-duplicate of Paginator with no clear optimization
findings.body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` and `value_from_cursor` are identical to `Paginator`. The `get_result` method is a copy of `BasePaginator.get_result` with the addition of the negative-offset path. There is no actual performance optimization present—no query plan hints, no deferred loading, no index optimization. The class adds maintenance burden and a dangerous code path without delivering the claimed benefit.

findings.title: Redirect loop limit reduced from 10000 to 1000 without explanation of safety
findings.body: The redirect resolution loop limit was reduced from 10000 to 1000. The removed comment explained that the limit means 'segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly.' Reducing to 1000 means traces with redirect chains deeper than 1000 will silently fail to merge, producing fragmented segments. While 1000-deep traces are rare, this is a silent data correctness regression with no metric or log to detect when the limit is hit.
